blocks.text: Fragile X syndrome is not associated with microorchidism. However, it is associated with macroorchidism. Macroorchidism becomes more evident during puberty and is a characteristic finding in males with fragile X syndrome.
Incorrect Options:

items.text: Option A - Trinucleotide mutation in FMR-1 gene: Fragile X syndrome is caused by an expansion of CGG trinucleotide repeats in the FMR-1 gene. This expansion leads to a decreased production of fragile X mental retardation protein (FMRP), resulting in the characteristic features of the syndrome.

Option B - Mental retardation: Intellectual disability is a hallmark feature of fragile X syndrome. It can range from mild to severe and is often associated with learning difficulties, speech and language delays, and behavioural challenges.
Option D - Large everted ears: Individuals with fragile X syndrome commonly exhibit large, prominent ears that are described as everted.

blocks.text: Consanguinity refers to a close blood relationship between the parents. Autosomal recessive diseases are more likely to occur in the offspring of consanguineous couples. This is because the parents may both carry a single copy of a recessive gene mutation, and when they have children together, there is an increased chance of both parents passing on the mutated gene, resulting in the expression of the disease phenotype in the offspring.
Incorrect Options:

items.text: Option B - Autosomal Dominant: Autosomal dominant diseases can occur in the offspring of consanguineous couples, but they are not specifically associated with consanguinity. Autosomal dominant diseases can also arise from de novo mutations or occur in non-consanguineous families.

Option C - X-Linked Recessive: X-linked recessive diseases are inherited through the X chromosome. Although consanguinity can increase the likelihood of inheriting X-linked recessive diseases, it is not the characteristic pattern associated with consanguinity.
Option D - X-Linked Dominant: X-linked dominant diseases can also occur in the offspring of consanguineous couples, but they are less common and not specifically associated with consanguinity.

blocks.text: G6PD deficiency is characterized by impaired function of the enzyme glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase. It follows an X-linked recessive pattern of inheritance.
Incorrect Options:

items.text: Option A - Hurler Syndrome: Hurler syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a deficiency of the enzyme alpha-L-iduronidase.
Option B - Thalassemia: Thalassemia is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner.
Option C - Hereditary Spherocytosis: Hereditary spherocytosis is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by abnormalities in red blood cell shape and function.

blocks.text: We differentiate benign and malignant tumours based on whether the basement membrane is intact or broken:
**In benign tumours:** The basement membrane is completely intact and normal.
**In malignant tumours:** The basement membrane is broken, so the cancer cells can invade surrounding tissues.

blocks.text: Teratomas arise from 2 or more germ layers
Teratomas are commonly seen in the ovaries, but can also be seen in other organs of the body.
Teratomas are of 2 types:

items.text: **Mature teratoma:** Benign and has all the mature tissues
**Immature teratoma:** Has neuroepithelial cells and has the potential to cause cancer.

blocks.text: Metaplasia is defined as the replacement of one type of epithelium with another. Metaplasia is 100% reversible. Until the trigger (GERD in this case) is present, metaplasia will stay, and metaplasia will be reversed when the trigger is treated.
The terminology of metaplasia is based on the end epithelium it forms. Intestinal columnar epithelium has goblet cells. Acidic mucin is present inside goblet cells, which is Alcian blue positive.
Barrett's esophagus is a precancerous condition, and if not treated, it may turn into Adenocarcinoma of esophagus.
Differentiation between precancer and cancer is based on the basement membrane.

items.text: If the basement membrane is intact: Precancer/Dysplasia
If the basement membrane is broken or breached: Cancer cells can invade into surrounding tissue and spread anywhere: Cancer/Anaplaisa

blocks.text: A hemangioma is a benign vascular tumour caused by an abnormal overgrowth of blood vessels that is distinguished from other benign tumours by:

items.text: Lack of well-defined capsule (Hemangiomas are uncapsulated).
Tendency to permeate the site of origin making it difficult for surgical excision.
**Rapid growth rate (Option A):** The rapid growth rate is a feature of malignant tumors, not benign tumors which grow slowly and localized to the site of origin.

**Presence of extracellular matrix (ECM) deposited by stromal cells (Option B):** Benign tumours usually has a capsule, which consists of an extracellular matrix (ECM) deposited by stromal cells such as fibroblasts. Since hemangioma is unencapsulated, it is not associated with the deposition of extracellular matrix by stromal cells.
**Easily resected by excision (Option C):** Encapsulation makes benign tumours easily resectable but since hemangiomas are unencapsulated,they permeate site of origin making it difficult to resect.

blocks.text: Metastasis means the distant spread of cancer. All cancers are capable of showing metastasis except 2 cancers, which show local invasion:

items.text: Basal cell cancer/Rodent's ulcer, which occurs on face.

**Sentinel lymph node (SLN):** The first lymph node to receive drainage from a primary tumor site. Example: In breast cancer, usually axillary lymph node is the first lymph node where the lymphatics are drained. Hence, it is the sentinel lymph node.

Sometimes, cancer may bypass the sentinel lymph node and spread directly to other lymph nodes. This can occur in patients who have received radiotherapy, as radiation can cause fibrosis and blockage of the lymphatic channels. If the pathway to the sentinel node is obstructed, tumour cells are diverted to alternative routes, resulting in what is known as skip metastasis.
Tumors where SLN biopsy is validated are Breast cancer, Melanoma, Vulvar cancer, and Colon cancer.

items.text: **The first lymph node to receive metastasis from a secondary tumour (Option A):** Sentinal lymph node is the first lymph node to receive drainage from a primary tumor site.
**Commonly involved in skip metastasis (Option C):** Skip metastasis is not a very common phenomenon; it's rather rare.
**The presence of cancer cells indicates a good prognosis (Option D):** Cancer spreading to the sentinel or any other lymph node is always a bad prognosis.

blocks.text: Occupational exposure to cadmium, commonly found in industries such as zinc mining, smelting of zinc ores, and battery manufacturing, has been associated with an increased risk of prostate cancer.

items.text: **Zinc (Option A):** Excessive zinc exposure does not have a direct association with prostate cancer.
**Benzopyrene (Option B):** It is associated with increased risks of lung cancer, bladder cancer, skin cancer, and other malignancies.
**Arsenic (Option C):** It is associated with an increased risk of angiosarcoma of the liver.
